    #42572. Here's How Much The 787 Dreamliner Heavily Influenced Boeing's 747-8 Development

    📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1640 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Simpleflying ↗ Open Full Page

    Here's How Much The 787 Dreamliner Heavily Influenced Boeing's 747-8 Development

    📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1640 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Simpleflying

    ⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent development, when Boeing launched the 747-8 in November 2005, it presented the airplane as a stretched, re-winged, and re-engined patch of the 747-400 that would use technology borrowed from the 787 Dreamliner.
    • In a recent development, rather than commissioning an all-newly introduced quadjet for a limited market, Boeing chose to graft selected Dreamliner innovations onto a familiar airframe, which kept development costs manageable and preserved the operating familiarity that long-time 747 customers valued.
    • The most substantial transfer from the 787 program came through the powerplants.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, when Boeing launched the 747-8 in November 2005, it presented the airplane as a stretched, re-winged, and re-engined patch of the 747-400 that would use technology borrowed from the 787 Dreamliner. The Dreamliner program had been launched only a year earlier, and its work on lightweight composites, efficient engines, and electronically managed systems gave Boeing a supply of proven solutions at the moment the aging jumbo needed them.

    In a recent development, rather than commissioning an all-newly introduced quadjet for a limited market, Boeing chose to graft selected Dreamliner innovations onto a familiar airframe, which kept development costs manageable and preserved the operating familiarity that long-time 747 customers valued. The resulting aircraft differs from its predecessor in several visible ways, yet it remains a 747 in its structure and in the way it is flown, so a fair assessment of the Dreamliner’s influence requires examining each major system in turn. That review shows a program that borrowed boldly where performance was at stake and conservatively wherever certification, cost, or pilot familiarity argued for restraint.

    Wikimedia Commons, Simple Flying.

    The most substantial transfer from the 787 program came through the powerplants. The 747-8 uses four General Electric GEnx-2B67 engines, a smaller-diameter relative of the GEnx developed for the Dreamliner. The design emphasizes a high bypass ratio, sending most of the air around the core to generate thrust more efficiently than the lower-bypass engines of earlier generations.

    Engineers modified the design so that each engine could supply bleed air, the compressed air tapped from the engine to run onboard systems, because the 747 still depends on a conventional pneumatic architecture that the 787 largely abandoned in favor of electrical power. Each engine generates 66,500 pounds (30,164 kg) of thrust and carries a 105-inch (267 cm) composite fan, a material choice that cuts weight relative to metallic blades.

    Recent findings suggest that GEnx-1B vs. GEnx-2B Technical Comparison.

    According to recent reports, sawtooth-shaped edges called chevrons line the rear of the engine housing, borrowing a noise-reduction device from the 787 that encourages exhaust and bypass air to blend more gradually. Noise also carries financial weight, since many airports levy charges tied to certified noise levels, and Boeing has said the 747-8 produces a considerably smaller noise footprint than the 747-400.

    In a recent development, sharing a design lineage with the 787 engine allowed Boeing and GE to spread development effort across two programs rather than funding a bespoke powerplant for a model expected to sell in modest numbers. Unlike the Dreamliner, which Boeing offers with a choice between GE and Rolls-Royce engines, the 747-8 is offered only with the GEnx-2B, which spared Boeing the cost of certifying a second powerplant for a modest order book. For operators, the engine change translated into lower fuel burn and emissions per seat than the 747-400, which formed the core of the airplane’s commercial pitch to airlines and cargo carriers.

    Boeing designed a new wing for the 747-8 with fresh airfoil shapes intended to improve aerodynamic efficiency at cruise. Designing a wing for a derivative airplane also imposes constraints that a clean-sheet program avoids, because the new surface had to mate with the existing fuselage architecture, which limited how far the planform could depart from the 747-400’s.

    Recent findings suggest that at the tips, the upright winglets of the 747-400 gave way to raked wingtips, the same approach used on the 777 and the 787. Sweeping the tip aft reduces drag generated by wingtip vortices while adding less weight than a taller vertical surface would. The configuration debuted on the 767-400ER, which means the 747-8 inherited it from a lineage broader than the Dreamliner alone.

    Boeing attributes the 747-8’s higher cruising speed relative to the 747-400 to the combined effect of the wing, wingtips, and engines. The gain matters to passenger carriers flying long routes, where minutes accumulate into meaningful time savings. The aerodynamic gains in cruise efficiency also translate directly into range or payload, which matters especially for the freighter, where operators trade fuel against cargo on long sectors.

    The larger wing extends the span to roughly 224 feet (68.27 meters), compared with about 211 feet (64.31 meters) on the 747-400, a growth that supports the airplane’s higher maximum takeoff weight. Aerodynamic refinement of this kind typically yields incremental gains, yet on an airplane that burns many tons of fuel on every long flight, even small improvements compound into sizable savings over a fleet’s life.

    Wikimedia Commons, Simple Flying.

    The 747-8 also adopted elements of the 787’s fly-by-wire philosophy, in which pilot inputs travel as electrical signals to flight control computers rather than moving surfaces through mechanical cables and pulleys. Electronic signaling reduces weight, since cable runs and associated hardware can be shortened, and it allows computers to modulate surface movements for smoother handling and greater structural efficiency.

    Sources indicate that the shift follows a broader pattern within the company, since the 777 was Boeing’s first fly-by-wire airliner and the 787 extended that approach more thoroughly. Boeing applied the technology selectively because it wanted qualified pilots on the 747-400 to move to the fresh model easily. The flight deck therefore keeps a layout and control feel close to its predecessor’s.

    Training pilots on an unfamiliar type requires simulator time, instructor capacity, and revenue flying hours that airlines would rather devote to scheduled service, so commonality functions as a quiet but substantial financial benefit for operators already flying the 747-400, whose crews can serve both types. The Dreamliner, by contrast, was free to adopt an entirely latest flight deck, a freedom the 747-8 deliberately did not exercise.

    Industry observers note that the passenger version of the 747-8 received an interior inspired by the Dreamliner’s. Curved, upswept ceiling panels give the cabin a more spacious feel, and LED lighting that runs the length of the cabin can shift color to suggest different times of day. Airlines adopt such lighting and ceiling cues largely because they believe the surroundings can ease fatigue on long sectors, though the benefit is difficult to measure objectively. Windows are larger than those on the 747-400, which improves natural light and passenger views, although they remain smaller than the Dreamliner’s distinctive dimmable windows.

    In a recent development, the most visible change for many travelers is the staircase to the upper deck. The classic 747’s narrow spiral staircase has been replaced by a wide, curved staircase that is easier to use and gives the entry area a more open, premium character. The interior upgrades arrived alongside an 18-foot-4-inch (5.5 meters) fuselage stretch, which lets Boeing quote a typical three-class capacity of 467 passengers. The stretch also lengthened the upper deck, giving airlines additional space for premium seating.

    Despite the heavy borrowing, the 747-8 does not share the Dreamliner’s defining structural feature. The 787 builds its fuselage from carbon fiber composites, whereas the 747-8 remains an aluminum airframe, consistent with the metallic construction of every earlier 747. The decision carries consequences that passengers can feel. Because composite structures resist corrosion and fatigue better than aluminum, the Dreamliner can maintain a lower cabin altitude and higher humidity than conventional metal airplanes, benefits the 747-8 does not offer.

    Recent findings suggest that retaining aluminum made commercial sense. A composite fuselage would have required a latest manufacturing process, new tooling, and a fresh certification effort for a program that was never expected to reach the volumes of a mainstream twin-aisle jet. Boeing instead reused the structure and production methods established over decades at its Everett factory, where the 747 had been built since the late 1960s.

    According to recent reports, boeing also preserved many systems in common with the 747-400, a choice that simplifies maintenance, spares provisioning, and mechanic training for airlines operating both models. The freighter, which accounts for the majority of 747-8 deliveries, retains the hinged nose door that lets long loads enter straight along the main deck.

    The 747-8 highlights that technology transfer, when applied with discipline and clear commercial goals, can extend an airframe’s commercial life without the expense of starting over. The final aircraft left the production line in early 2023 after 155 had been built. Its more durable influence may appear in cargo operations, where the freighters seem likely to remain in service for decades. Few alternatives offer comparable volume, and the Dreamliner-derived engines should keep operating costs competitive as fleets age in the years ahead.

    It has been revealed that sustainable aviation fuel offers a further lever for extending service lives, because engines of the GEnx generation are approved for blends with conventional jet fuel, which lets operators reduce lifecycle emissions without modifying the airplane. Market pressure shapes what comes next, since fuel efficiency and emissions goals increasingly favor twin-engine aircraft, so the quadjet is unlikely to return as a clean-sheet design, and the 747-8’s lasting contribution may be as the final demonstration of how far a four-engine airliner could be pushed with the technology of its time.

    It has been revealed that the 747-8 program also previews how Boeing is likely to modernize mature designs in the future. The 777X, for example, pairs a newly introduced composite wing with new engines on a fuselage descended from the 777, a pattern that mirrors the 747-8’s selective borrowing but moves much further toward composite structure. For engineers, the more transferable lesson concerns what to share and what to withhold.

    In a recent development, components that improve efficiency without altering certification basis or pilot procedures, such as engines, aerodynamic surfaces, and lighting, moved across freely, while anything that would have disrupted commonality with the 747-400 stayed behind. Future derivatives are likely to follow the same filter, with the cost of recertification acting as the main gatekeeper, and the 747-8 supplies the clearest template of that logic.

    Amex Graphite Business Cash Unlimited Card Review: Is The $295 Fee Worth It?

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 15 min read (2962 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Onemileatatime

    ⏱️ ~15 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • The Graphite™ Business Cash Unlimited Card rolled out in March 2026.
    • However, there are some things that could make this card worthwhile, including a potentially lucrative welcome offer, a solid return on spending, and some credits that can help offset the annual fee.
    • According to recent reports, this post is my in-depth Amex Graphite Business Cash Unlimited review.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The Graphite™ Business Cash Unlimited Card rolled out in March 2026. On the surface, the card sounds rather uncompetitive — it has a $295 annual fee (Rates & Fees), and offers “just” 2% cash back on everyday spending, with limited bonus categories.

    However, there are some things that could make this card worthwhile, including a potentially lucrative welcome offer, a solid return on spending, and some credits that can help offset the annual fee. If your business spends a lot, you value having an Amex, and you just want to earn simple cash back without a complex rewards structure, this could be a good option.

    According to recent reports, this post is my in-depth Amex Graphite Business Cash Unlimited review. Is the card worth it, and if so, under what circumstances? And what are the best alternatives?

    Link: Learn more about the Graphite™ Business Cash Unlimited Card.

    Before I get into my Amex Graphite Business Cash Unlimited review, let me briefly summarize the key details of the card:.

    Beyond that, here are what I consider to be some of the major pros and cons of the Amex Graphite Business Cash Unlimited:.

    It has been revealed that with the above out of the way, let’s look at the various aspects of the Amex Graphite Business Cash Unlimited, from the welcome offer, to the fees, to the rewards structure, to the other perks. This card is fairly straightforward, so there’s not all that much to understand, for better or worse.

    Sources indicate that the Amex Graphite Business Cash Unlimited at the moment has a welcome offer where you can earn as high as $2,000 cash back after spending $50,000 within the first six months on eligible purchases. Reward Dollars can be redeemed as statement credits to offset transactions, or as a payment method for Amazon purchases.

    Given that the card ordinarily offers at least 2% cash back, that means spending $50,000 could earn you a minimum of $3,000 (if offered the full bonus amount), equivalent to 6% cash back on that amount of spending, which is solid.

    According to recent reports, admittedly the spending requirement is major (it averages out to $8,333 per month over the course of six months), but I do think businesses that spend a lot might find this to be achievable. Furthermore, it’s nice that you have six months to complete the spending requirement, while many other cards give you only three months to reach the spending requirement.

    If you’re applying for the Amex Graphite Business Cash Unlimited, be aware of Amex’s general restrictions on applying for cards, including the “once in a lifetime rule.” That means you’re not eligible for the welcome offer on the card if you’ve already had this card, though you are potentially eligible for the bonus if you’ve had other Amex cards.

    Industry observers note that anecdotally, I find Amex business cards to be quite easy to get approved for. I also love how with Amex, you can know if you’ll be approved with no credit score impact — the hard pull only happens after you’re told if you’re approved, and you accept the offer.

    Also keep in mind that if you’re concerned about staying under Chase’s 5/24 limit, applying for an Amex business card won’t count toward that, since it doesn’t show up on your personal credit report in that way.

    Sources indicate that when it comes to credit score, there’s not a consistent credit score you need to get approved for the card, as it’s one of only many factors that determines eligibility. Personally, I’d hope to have a score in the “good” to “excellent” range, ideally 700+ points. However, people with lower scores have been approved, and people with higher scores have been rejected.

    The Amex Graphite Business Cash Unlimited has an annual fee of $295 (Rates & Fees), which is definitely on the steep side, especially given the relatively narrow appeal of the credits offered on the card, which require a lot of spending.

    With the card’s 2% cash back rewards structure, you’d essentially recoup the annual fee (in terms of rewards) after $14,750 in spending.

    In a recent development, the Amex Graphite Business Cash Unlimited has an authorized user fee of $95 for the first 5 cards, and a $95 annual fee for each thereafter (Rates & Fees), though you can also get a no annual fee Employee Business Expense Card with no additional fee. Still, that’s a rather steep authorized user fee for a card that doesn’t actually offer many incremental perks. You can add up to 99 employee cards to your account.

    The Amex Graphite Business Cash Unlimited has no preset spending limit. The idea is that this gives you flexibility in ways that traditional credit cards don’t. The amount you can spend adapts based on factors such as your purchase, payment, and credit history. Rather than having a set limit, you could grow your purchasing power the more you consistently use your card and regularly make payments.

    In fairness, it is also worth mentioning that not having a preset spending limit can also lead to some declines if the amount you can charge decreases, so it’s a little less predictable than a regular credit card. However, I find that more often than not, it works in the favor of cardmembers.

    Industry observers note that no Preset Spending Limit means your spending limit is flexible. Unlike a traditional card with a set limit, the amount you can spend adapts based on factors such as your purchase, payment, and credit history.

    In terms of its rewards structure, the Amex Graphite Business Cash Unlimited offers 2% cash back on eligible purchases. On top of that, the card offers 5% cash back on flights and prepaid hotels booked through American Express Travel® Online. Just to do some very basic math:.

    Sources indicate that all cash back on the card is earned as Reward Dollars, which can be redeemed as statement credits to offset transactions, or as a payment method for Amazon purchases. Unfortunately there are no other redemption options, so you couldn’t directly deposit the cash back into a business checking account, or anything like that.

    2% cash back on credit card spending is the “gold standard,” as I see it, so that’s excellent, and what everyone should be aiming for, at a minimum.

    Meanwhile the 5% cash back on Amex Travel might sound appealing, but there are some catches. If you can route travel spending that way, it’s a good option, but the catch is that you may sometimes find lower rates elsewhere, so there could be an opportunity cost to booking that way.

    Sources indicate that the Amex Graphite Business Cash Unlimited offers up to $2,400 in American Express One AP® statement credits, after spending $250,000 on eligible purchases on the card in a calendar year. Statement credits will be applied to the monthly bill charged to the card for Amex’s accounts payable solution, One AP, for the following calendar year, and this includes an auto-renewing platform access fee.

    American Express One AP® is an accounts payable solution that can help transform the way your business pays suppliers. With One AP, you can streamline your supplier invoice payments on a single platform and pay by virtual card, check, and ACH. Enrollment is required.

    It has been revealed that this program charges a $200 monthly fee to pay vendors with non-cards, plus has a fee for checks and ACHs over a certain limit. So the $2,400 annual credit can potentially fully cover your monthly fee. While this is potentially a nice feature, keep in mind that many platforms already offer this as a built in feature at no extra cost, so it’s not really that special.

    The Amex Graphite Business Cash Unlimited offers the Pay Over Time feature, whereby cardmembers can carry a balance with interest on eligible charges, up to the Pay Over Time limit. The way this works, eligible charges will automatically be added to a Pay Over Time balance, up to the Pay Over Time limit.

    It has been revealed that you can choose to pay for these charges over time with interest, or you can pay your full balance each month, whichever is best for your business. You must pay in full any charge or a portion of a charge that is not added to a Pay Over Time balance.

    Personally, I recommend paying the balance in full each billing cycle if possible, to avoid interest charges, especially given how high they can be. However, I think it’s worth clarifying that the Pay Over Time option is possible, given that this isn’t a traditional credit card.

    It has been revealed that it’s also worth emphasizing the difference between the Pay Over Time and the Pay In Full Limit. The latter could be an amount that has to be paid in full, and there’s no option to pay that over time with interest charges.

    Industry observers note that the Amex Graphite Business Cash Card earns 2% cash back, and I consider that to be the minimum “gold standard” of credit card rewards. So the card’s rewards structure is perfectly fine. The 5% cash back on travel is also pretty limiting, given that you have to book through Amex.

    I think the matter is the steep annual fee, given that there are also much more affordable (and even no annual fee) cards with that kind of a rewards structure. In fairness, Amex doesn’t have another business card earning unlimited 2% cash back. It’s just not a upcoming concept more broadly, and there are lots of competing cards that I’d consider to be superior.

    Recent findings suggest that so who should consider the card? As I see it, the Amex Graphite Business Cash Card is targeted at a specific demographic. This card could make sense for the following types of customers:.

    In a recent development, I do truly think this is a niche product. But the idea is that if you’re a small business owner charging hundreds of thousands or millions of dollars on credit cards per year, that annual fee won’t make much of a difference.

    Still, I’d like to compare this to some other popular products, as I think there are other cards that may be a better fit for some other people.

    It has been revealed that perhaps the best direct comparison to the Amex Graphite Business Cash Card is The American Express Blue Business Cash® Card (learn more). The card has no annual fee (Rates & Fees) and offers 2% cash back on the first $50,000 spent every calendar year (and 1% cash back thereafter).

    In a recent development, the upside here is obvious, as you’re earning 2% cash back with no fee. The downside is that the welcome offer is much smaller (though also with a smaller spending requirement), the card has foreign transaction fees, you’re capped at earning 2% cash back on the first $50,000 spent annually, and the card does have a preset spending limit.

    For a small business mostly spending money domestically, the Amex Blue Business Cash is a great alternative to the Amex Graphite Business Cash.

    Recent findings suggest that another potential alternative to the Amex Graphite Business Cash Card is The Blue Business® Plus Credit Card from American Express (learn more). The card has no annual fee (Rates & Fees) and offers 2x Membership Rewards points on the first $50,000 spent every calendar year (and 1x points thereafter).

    Recent findings suggest that if you’re good at redeeming points, that’s a pretty incredible return, since based on my latest miles & points valuations, Amex points are worth 1.7 cents each, for a return of up to 3.4%. The downsides to the Amex Blue Business Plus are otherwise identical to those on the Amex Blue Business Cash — the welcome offer is much smaller (though also with a smaller spending requirement), the card has foreign transaction fees, you’re capped at earning 2x points on the first $50,000 spent annually, and the card does have a preset spending limit.

    So the card is either useful if $50,000 covers your annual business spending, or you’re willing to use another card after you hit that initial $50,000 spending cap.

    Speaking of premium Amex business cards, it’s also worth comparing the Amex Graphite Business Cash Card to the American Express® Business Gold Card (learn more). The Amex Business Gold has a $375 annual fee (Rates & Fees), and offers an incredible rewards structure (with up to 4x Membership Rewards points in select categories), plus statement credits that can greatly help offset the annual fee.

    As I see it, the Amex Graphite Business Cash Card is the better option if you value cash back and a straightforward rewards structure, while the Amex Business Gold is the better option if you can take advantage of the bonus categories, and are willing to put in the effort to maximize points.

    While the above comparisons are all to Amex cards, I think it’s also worth comparing the Amex Graphite Business Cash Card to the Capital One Spark Cash Plus (learn more), as it’s perhaps the most direct competitor.

    Recent findings suggest that the card has a massive welcome offer of $2,000 cash back after spending $30,000 within the first three months (plus an additional $2,000 cash back bonus for every $500,000 spent during the first year), offers 5% cash back on select Capital One Business Travel purchases and 2% cash back with no caps and no foreign transaction fees on other purchases, and it has a $150 annual fee. Furthermore, the card offers an annual bonus of $150 if you spend at least $150,000 on the card in a calendar year, essentially rebating the annual fee.

    I do think the Capital One Spark Cash Plus is more compelling than the Amex Graphite Business Cash Card on balance, unless you specifically have a reason you’d like an Amex, or value the statement credits tied to spending $250,000 per year.

    I’d also like to compare the Amex Graphite Business Cash Card to the Ink Business Premier® Credit Card (learn more), as it’s another potentially lucrative cash back card.

    Recent findings suggest that in addition to a substantial welcome offer of $1,000 cash back after spending $10,000 within the first three months, the card offers 5% cash back on Chase Travel purchases, 2.5% cash back on purchases of $5,000 or more, and 2% cash back on all other purchases, with no foreign transaction fees, and it has a $195 annual fee. So if you have a business that frequently makes large purchases, the Chase Ink Business Premier could be a great alternative.

    In a recent development, the Amex Graphite Business Cash Card has a $295 annual fee, and offers unlimited 2% cash back, with no preset spending limit, plus a large welcome offer.     💡 Key Takeaways
    • Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., holds a news conference in the Capitol on Nov.
    • Saying that “Medicare for All” is no longer “a radical idea,” Sen.
    • Industry observers note that democrats could bring it about through the filibuster-proof budget reconciliation process, the Vermont independent and avowed democratic socialist told reporters.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., holds a news conference in the Capitol on Nov. 10. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call).

    Saying that “Medicare for All” is no longer “a radical idea,” Sen. Bernie Sanders said Wednesday that he would prioritize passing the universal health care initiative if he assumes the chairmanship of the Health, Education, Labor and Pensions Committee next year as expected.

    Industry observers note that democrats could bring it about through the filibuster-proof budget reconciliation process, the Vermont independent and avowed democratic socialist told reporters. And the idea could be buoyed by an influx of progressive lawmakers elected in the midterms.

    Recent findings suggest that sanders mentioned Medicare for All is gaining support from voters across the country who are looking to overhaul the American health care system as costs have soared. Democrats on the committee will move the legislation “as aggressively as we can, as rapidly as we can,” he said.

    Sources indicate that his version, introduced in April and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, would implement the universal health care system over four years. In the first year, the the age of Medicare eligibility would drop to 55 from 65, while coverage would expand to include dental, hearing and vision care. The bill would also provide coverage for eligible children during the first year.

    The age of eligibility would fall another 10 years in each of the following years until the fourth year, when coverage would be extended to all Americans.

    “If there has ever been a time in the modern history of our country . . . to address the crises facing working families, this is that time,” Sanders stated, noting that Democrats will have a 56-44 majority when the 120th Congress begins in January, the largest margin for either party in 16 years.

    Sen. Tammy Baldwin, D-Wis., along with nine other Senate Democrats, last week offered an alternative Medicare expansion blueprint, which would lower the eligibility to those ages 50 and up.

    While who will be leading Senate Democrats is still an open question — Chris Van Hollen of Maryland is challenging Charles E. Schumer of New York, who has been the top Senate Democrat since 2017 — Sanders noted he is confident the Medicare for All bill will get to the Senate floor, “no matter who the [Senate majority] leader is.” Sanders previously expressed opposition to Schumer leading the conference.

    Asked about efforts to extend the Affordable Care Act enhanced subsidies, Sanders responded he’s “all in.” However, he added “the American people and elected officials understand the current health care system is broken.”.

    Subsidies that help enrollees pay for health care premiums on the ACA exchanges were expanded during the COVID-19 pandemic, but these enhanced credits expired at the end of last year, raising costs for many who relied on them to help defray costs.

    House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, nominated on Wednesday to be speaker next year, previously outlined broader health care priorities such as extending the ACA tax credits and reversing Medicaid cuts enacted in Republicans' reconciliation package last year. When asked Tuesday how far Democrats want to lower the Medicare eligibility age, Jeffries responded, “that’s all part of an ongoing conversation.”.

    Industry observers note that in addition to expanding Medicare coverage, Sanders reiterated his push to lower prescription drug prices. The Vermont lawmaker previously introduced legislation aimed at reducing the cost of brand name prescription drugs by linking domestic prices to international price benchmarks.

    To enact some of the agenda, Sanders may have to court Republicans.

    In a recent development, sen. Rand Paul, R-Ky., noted last week that he plans to serve as the top Republican on the HELP committee next year. Sanders said Wednesday that his likely GOP counterpart “has shown an enormous amount of courage in taking on Republican leadership year after year.”.

    Sanders added that although Paul may have a different viewpoint from himself on committee issues, he looks forward to finding common ground.

    #42567. The Plot to Overthrow the Electoral College Must Fail

    📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1618 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Nationalreview ↗ Open Full Page

    The Plot to Overthrow the Electoral College Must Fail

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1618 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nationalreview

    ⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Article II, Section 1 of the Constitution sets out the process by which Americans select their president.
    • Democrats have been railing against the Electoral College since losing the 2000 and 2016 elections while winning a plurality of the popular vote.
    • A proposed workaround has sailed through the legislatures of 18 blue states and the District of Columbia: the National Popular Vote Interstate Compact.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Article II, Section 1 of the Constitution sets out the process by which Americans select their president. Alexander Hamilton marveled at the time, in Federalist No. 68, that it was “almost the only part of the system, of any consequence, which has escaped without severe censure, or which has received the slightest mark of approbation from its opponents.” The core of that process is that the members of the Electoral College are selected in each state. With only the Twelfth Amendment’s modification in 1804 to adjust how the vice president is selected, this same system has been in continuous use for 238 years. It is how George Washington, Abraham Lincoln, Franklin D. Roosevelt, Ronald Reagan, and Barack Obama were elected. Now, a nefarious plot aims to overthrow the American system.

    Democrats have been railing against the Electoral College since losing the 2000 and 2016 elections while winning a plurality of the popular vote. These partisan sour grapes have often been dismissed as empty talk because the Electoral College is established by the Constitution, so only an amendment could abolish it. An amendment requires a two-thirds vote of Congress and the consent of 38 states, both of which are out of reach on a party-line vote.

    A proposed workaround has sailed through the legislatures of 18 blue states and the District of Columbia: the National Popular Vote Interstate Compact. The theory is that these states would award their electors not to the winner of the popular vote in their own state, but to the winner of the national popular vote. It may be that a state can decide on its own to do this. States have not always picked electors by statewide popular vote. Many states at the Founding had their state legislatures choose electors. South Carolina did so all the way to the Civil War. Colorado in 1876 was the last state to do so, but only because it had just been admitted to statehood and claimed not to have time to organize a statewide vote. Other states have awarded electors to the winners of each House district, as Maine and Nebraska do today; this system was upheld by the Supreme Court in 1892.

    Industry observers note that but the National Popular Vote Interstate Compact is not just a unilateral decision by individual states about how to award their electors. If it had been, it would already have been effective in 2024, and Donald Trump would have won the Electoral College 530–8 with 49.7 percent of the popular vote. Instead, it is styled as an agreement that goes into effect only if states composing a majority of the Electoral College approve it. At present, the signatories control 222 electoral votes. With Democrats gaining trifectas in Pennsylvania, Michigan, Wisconsin, Nevada, and Arizona, they conceivably could pass the compact in states controlling 283 electoral votes. They also now control the Fresh Hampshire state legislature, although with a veto-proof majority only in one of its two chambers, they would have to get through Republican Governor Kelly Ayotte.

    In a recent development, passage is not certain. Michigan Democrats have previously rejected the compact in 2023 and 2024, and in Nevada (a smaller state that would be swamped under the compact), the Democratic governor vetoed it in 2019. Some of the small-state signatories, such as Delaware, Vermont, Rhode Island, or Upcoming Mexico, might yet have second thoughts now that they are playing with live ammunition.

    It has been revealed that moreover, under Article I, Section 10, interstate compacts require the consent of Congress. Even if Democrats passed it in the next two years with the aim of changing the rules for the 2028 election, Trump would surely veto it. After the 2030 Census, a number of the signatory states are expected to lose House seats, which will further narrow the margin for keeping it in effect. Then, there’s the question of whether the Supreme Court would allow individual states to gang up and effectively nullify the entire constitutional design of our presidential election system.

    According to recent reports, legal obstacles aside, this is a bad idea. To start with, the very durability of our system over such a long period is an argument in its favor. No other nation has used the same system for choosing its head of state and government for so long. Leaving aside the dubious precedents of 1824 (when popular vote records were not kept in the most populous state) and 1876 (when fraud was rampant in both parties and Southern Democrats engaged in mass violence against Republican voters), the Electoral College has only delivered a different outcome from the national popular vote three times in our history. In each case, the national vote was fairly close and neither candidate got a popular majority, so the Electoral College provided the legitimacy of a majority result that the popular vote could not. This may have frustrated Californians, but it was not just the tyranny of a few small places with no people in them. In 2016, Trump won the popular vote in seven of the ten largest states. It is nearly impossible to win a national popular majority without carrying the Electoral College.

    Industry observers note that we have an Electoral College because we are a nation of diverse and distinct states. The American people are long accustomed to this system. The people ratified the Constitution and its amendments state-by-state. The Senate is elected by the people in states, the House by people in districts. Both political parties choose their presidential nominees by primary elections in each state. Americans have never before held a nationwide popular vote for any purpose. Our election systems, run by state and local officials with a variety of rules for the timing of casting and counting ballots and for confirming the qualifications of voters, are not designed for such a vote.

    In a recent development, our campaigns today still prioritize appeals to the most closely divided states. This encourages presidential candidates to pitch at least some of their message to voters in the center, and also to travel the country in order to garner coverage in statewide media and the support of state and local power brokers. A national popular vote campaign would drive us even further down the road of nationalizing the campaign media environment and encouraging candidates to rally voters in their party’s strongholds. It would also exacerbate the divide between urban and rural or small-town America, given how the largest cities could effectively ally themselves against their own in-state neighbors.

    Industry observers note that few of the world’s democracies conduct a nationwide vote for the chief executive. In France, which is one of those, the first man to win such a vote seized power in a coup before his first term ended. National popular plebiscites are far more common in dictatorial systems, where the president has more control over who counts the votes. One of the reasons why the January 6 mob was never a serious threat to overturn the 2020 election was that the state-by-state winners had already been publicly certified in 50 separate state capitals. This was a deliberate feature of the system: As Hamilton wrote, “as the electors, chosen in each State, are to assemble and vote in the State in which they are chosen, this detached and divided situation will expose them much less to heats and ferments . . . than if they were all to be convened at one time, in one place.”.

    We would inevitably need to overhaul our entire election system to accommodate a nationwide vote. It is not a coincidence that such a nationalization of elections is favored by many of the same people who want to do away with the Electoral College. As things stand today, the whole country would have to wait on California, which not only takes weeks to count votes, but does so in order to count late-arriving ballots and to “cure” defective ballots — a process bound to erode confidence in a close election. That matters little when nobody doubts the outcome in California. But by making elections turn on the margins of victory in the deepest-blue or deepest-red jurisdictions, whose election officials are uniformly of the same party, the incentives for all manner of electoral malfeasance would be supercharged.

    Industry observers note that the 1888 election provides a vivid, if extreme, example of how the Electoral College limits the scope of mischief done by the corruption of voting systems in particular states. The eleven states of the former Confederacy were then well into the post-Reconstruction suppression of the black vote in their states. As a result, the Democratic nominee, Grover Cleveland, won those states by almost 25 points, with over 60 percent of the vote. This propelled Cleveland to a narrow plurality in the national popular vote even though his Republican opponent, Benjamin Harrison, won a popular majority in the rest of the country. Yet the Electoral College gave Harrison the victory because his support was not as concentrated in an unrepresentative handful of states in which the vote was compromised.

    Industry observers note that if a nationwide vote would be a headache, a nationwide recount would be a nightmare. Nobody who lived through the 2000 and 2020 post-election controversies should have any illusions that such a thing could be conducted in a civil and orderly fashion in today’s America. Rather than wait to learn that lesson the hard way, we should step back from the brink of overthrowing the system that has chosen our nation’s leader from the beginning.

    The Editors comprise the senior editorial staff of National Review magazine and nationalreview.com.

    On “The Plot to Overthrow the Electoral College Must Fail”.

    📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1171 w)

    Most Airports Cap Concession Prices… But The System Is A Total Joke

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1171 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Onemileatatime

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Travelers are conditioned to expect high prices at airport retailers and restaurants, so over $5 for a bottle of water at an airport shop, or $25 for a burger at a mediocre airport restaurant, might not catch anyone off guard.
    • According to recent reports, however, did you know there are caps on how much retailers at airports are supposed to be able to charge, and they’re largely just not enforced?
    • Industry observers note that airports generate revenue in a variety of ways, and one of the major ways is through the retailers they have in the terminal.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Travelers are conditioned to expect high prices at airport retailers and restaurants, so over $5 for a bottle of water at an airport shop, or $25 for a burger at a mediocre airport restaurant, might not catch anyone off guard.

    According to recent reports, however, did you know there are caps on how much retailers at airports are supposed to be able to charge, and they’re largely just not enforced? Well, or perhaps more accurately, they are enforced, but using very dishonest math. The backstory of this is interesting.

    Industry observers note that airports generate revenue in a variety of ways, and one of the major ways is through the retailers they have in the terminal. An airport is like a shopping mall with a very captive audience, and as you’d expect, rent for businesses in airports is absolutely through the roof, as a result of that.

    But in order to balance things out and prevent retailers from exploiting consumers, over 80% of airports in the United States specifically stipulate the maximum prices that airports can charge consumers. These terms are typically baked into the contracts that airport retailers sign, and failure to adhere to the rules can lead to consequences, at least in theory.

    The airports with pricing caps for airport businesses generally fall into one of two categories:.

    If there are supposed to be rules in place capping airport pricing, then why is this such a widespread glitch? More Perfect Union recently published a great video investigating this issue, and it’s a fascinating watch. First they actually analyze airport pricing, and then they confront airport authorities about the lack of enforcement.

    Here’s what’s interesting — airport retailers do have to submit comparisons for benchmark pricing, to prove that they’re not violating rules and exploiting customers. The problem is what kind of businesses are considered comparable for the purposes of “street pricing.”.

    For example, 9NEWS recently investigated this at Denver Airport, finding that a basic Starbucks coffee cost $4.55 in the airport, compared to $2.95 outside the airport (a 54% markup), and a bag of cashews cost $9.99 in the airport, compared to $4.74 outside the airport (a 110% markup).

    The airport’s VP of Concessions agreed to sit down with the reporter to discuss this, and she mentioned the results of his investigation were great news — she suggested that 93% of the prices were compliant, and said “that’s pretty darn good.” How could that be, given the high markups compared to nearby businesses?

    The matter boils down to how much latitude businesses have to submit pricing comparisons:.

    What’s wild is how the airport official responds to Starbucks just having consistent pricing, and violating the rules:.

    VP of Concessions: “What I get from that is, they’re looking for consistency, across the board, across the nation, across the world.”Reporter: “I can’t help but think that travelers may be looking for consistency, but if they see a cheaper cup of coffee, they’ll probably be okay with it.”VP of Concessions: “I don’t know the answer to that. This is how we take care of our passengers, by ensuring that they are paying fair and transparent pricing, while supporting our business partners.”.

    Back to the original story, the More Perfect Union reporter confronted the Port Authority of New York and New Jersey about pricing like $6.89 for one liter of Smart Water, compared to closer to $3.50 at nearby bodegas.

    The response was that “comparing a Hudson to a bodega isn’t appropriate,” because “Hudson is a specialty market.” The approved price comparison was reportedly based on the price of water at Tablet Works, a “wellness & concierge pharmacy” in a high-end mall.

    Recent findings suggest that the other thing to keep in mind is that a large percentage of airport retailers and restaurants are run by the same few companies, like HMSHost, which is a subsidiary of Avolta. So clearly they have a centralized approach to submitting pricing comparisons, and know exactly what they’re doing. Interestingly, the few independent businesses in some airports were found to have the most honest pricing.

    Sources indicate that so to sum it up, the system is designed to be rigged. Airport authorities can technically pretend they’re looking out for consumers by setting a cap. Retailers can submit pricing comparisons to the highest prices they can find anywhere. Then airport authorities verify those prices to pretend they’re doing their jobs.

    Recent findings suggest that airports are obviously complicit in all of this. They make money by charging sky high rent, and the reason they can do that is because retailers can charge hugely inflated prices. The more profits retailers make, the more airports can charge in rent. And they know that no consumer is going to avoid an airport because of high concession costs.

    Around 80% of airports in the United States cap the prices that retailers can charge, so in most cases, you’re not supposed to be paying more than 15% above “street pricing.” The matter is the liberties that businesses can take with what constitutes “street pricing.”.

    In a recent development, the price of the bottle of water or smoothie you’re buying isn’t compared to what you’d pay at a nearby gas station and smoothie shop, but instead, is being compared to what you’d pay at Erewhon. Talk about a very broken system, with no incentives for any party to actually be honest….

    What do you make of this airport pricing situation?

    #42563. Is It True That The Boeing 747-8 & 787 Dreamliner Are Powered By The Same Engine?

    Is It True That The Boeing 747-8 & 787 Dreamliner Are Powered By The Same Engine?

    📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1352 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Simpleflying

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It is true that both the 747-8, the final iteration of the Boeing double-decker, and the 787 Dreamliner, its latest and greatest clean sheet design, use the same engine.
    • The 747-8 exclusively uses the GEnx-2B while the 787 Dreamliner is the only jetliner to ever be equipped with the GEnx-1B.
    • For airlines that operate both the 787 and 747-8, using the same engine family simplifies maintenance, parts inventory, and technician training.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It is true that both the 747-8, the final iteration of the Boeing double-decker, and the 787 Dreamliner, its latest and greatest clean sheet design, use the same engine. However, each of these aircraft uses a different variation of that same turbofan that is tailored to its unique needs and engineering qualities.

    The 747-8 exclusively uses the GEnx-2B while the 787 Dreamliner is the only jetliner to ever be equipped with the GEnx-1B. Boeing chose the GEnx for the 747-8 primarily to modernize the aging jumbo jet with next-generation technology. Both aircraft feature distinctive serrated chevrons on the engine nacelles, which mix hot exhaust with cool air to significantly reduce noise.

    For airlines that operate both the 787 and 747-8, using the same engine family simplifies maintenance, parts inventory, and technician training. The GEnx-1B is a larger, more powerful, and more-electric engine designed for a modern twin-engine jet. The GEnx-2B is a smaller, simplified variant that incorporates traditional pneumatics to breathe life into the older 747 systems while providing modern fuel efficiency.

    In a recent development, while the GEnx-1B (787) and GEnx-2B (747-8) share a common high-pressure core and 80% of their Line Replaceable Units, they are distinct engines optimized for different aircraft architectures. The most fundamental difference is how the engines interact with the aircraft's internal systems. The GEnx family is designed to stay on wing 20% longer than previous generations, with some fleet leaders exceeding 30,000 hours without a major overhaul.

    Both engines offer approximately 15% better fuel efficiency than the older CF6 engines they replaced. Tom Levin, General Manager of the GEnx/CF6 engine product line at GE Aviation, commented on the engine's success when the 1,000th GEnx engine was developed in 2015.

    “The GEnx was the fastest selling engine in GE’s history, and now it is the fastest production ramp up of a GE widebody engine program. The GEnx engine has proven itself with outstanding performance and reliability.".

    In a recent development, the 787 uses a bleedless architecture where most systems are powered electrically. The 747-8 uses a traditional bleed-air system to power environmental controls and start the engines, requiring the GEnx-2B to include bleed-air ports. The GEnx-2B has fewer stages in the booster and low-pressure turbine, optimizing it for a four-engine configuration.

    It has been revealed that the Boeing 747-8, on the other hand, uses a traditional bleed air system. It must bleed high-pressure air from the compressor to power the 747’s pneumatic systems, including cabin pressurization and thermal anti-icing.

    Recent findings suggest that to fit the 747’s wing and ground clearance, the GEnx-2B has a smaller fan diameter, 105 inches, compared to the 787’s 111 inches. Because the 747-8 has four engines while the 787 has only two, the -2B is simplified internally to be lighter and more optimized for its lower per-engine thrust requirement. The -2B produces roughly 66,500 lbs of thrust, whereas the 787 variants can reach up to 76,100 lbs.

    The GEnx-1B has more power because it is intended for a twin-engine aircraft (787) that must maintain performance in the event of an engine failure during takeoff. Because the GEnx-2B's power is distributed across four engines on the 747-8, its thrust rating is 66,500 lbf lower. Compared with older engines like the CF6, the GEnx-2B's technology improves fuel efficiency and cuts emissions by 15%.

    In a recent development, in contrast to the 1B, the GEnx-2B has de-staged components to maximize weight and performance for a four-engine setup. In contrast to the 1B's four stages, the 2B's low-pressure compressor has three stages. In the low-pressure turbine, the 1B has seven stages, whereas the 2B has six.

    Industry observers note that compared with the 747-8, the 787 Dreamliner delivers bettereconomics and is much more efficient in the widebody market, as it is a lightweight twin-engine composite aircraft. These engineering variations determine their efficiency and commercial success. The 747 uses about 3,800 gallons of fuel per hour, while the 787 uses about 2,900 gallons. The 787-9 is extremely efficient, using approximately 2.31 liters per 100 km per passenger, which is significantly better than the 747-8's 2.82 liters per 100 km per passenger.

    According to recent reports, boeing's Dreamliner also costs significantly less to operate, with a lower cost per available seat mile. Airlines typically prefer smaller twin-engine aircraft because they are less dangerous to fill and fly. The 787's design and performance have allowed it to thrive in the modern aviation market, while the 747-8 saw limited passenger orders before production ended in 2017 and the 747 assembly line fully shut down in 2023.

    Recent findings suggest that the Dreamliner has essentially eliminated the conventional hub-and-spoke paradigm that made the 747 necessary. While the 747 required high passenger capacity to be successful, the 787's efficiency lets it cover the same distances with fewer seats, making it a better match for today's point-to-point market.

    The 787's efficiency allows airlines to launch newly introduced, nonstop point-to-point routes that would not have been economically viable with older, bigger, four-engine planes. Despite being more efficient than previous 747s, the 747-8 is still best suited to high-volume hub-to-hub services. Airlines such as United have made large 787 orders to replace a mix of 747s, 767s, and early 777s with a single, simpler aircraft family, resulting in significant cost savings for pilot training and component inventory.

    Industry observers note that the 787 incorporates a large amount of carbon composite material, making it lighter, more resistant to fatigue and corrosion, and allowing for higher cabin humidity and lower cabin altitude, which enhances passenger comfort and reduces structural stress. The 747-8 is a development of a traditional aluminum design, with a heavier base structure.

    Lufthansa has incorporated the 787-9 to handle flights that need the same range but have about 70–90 fewer people, even though it is still a 747-8 operator. Because of this, even at off-peak times, the airline can maintain high load factors (percentage of seats filled). British Airways switched to the 787-10 for vital transatlantic flights to Newly introduced York and Chicago after retiring its entire 747 fleet. The 787-10 is 25% more fuel-efficient than the 747 while offering comparable cargo capacity and contemporary comforts.

    Compared to the 747, the 787 Dreamliner offers a better long-haul passenger experience because its composite airframe creates a cabin environment that more closely resembles ground conditions. When compared to older aircraft like the 747, which have a cabin altitude of 8,000 feet, the 787's cabin altitude of 6,000 feet makes a significant difference for passengers. That lower cabin altitude does many things to reduce the effects of fatigue on passengers inflight.

    The composite construction of the 787 is not only 50% by weight but 80% by volume. Thanks to that light yet incredibly durable construction, it can do things no previous aircraft could. That includes having larger windows, higher humidity (15% or double that of legacy jets), and a more spacious interior with more natural lighting and better overhead storage.

    In a recent development, while the 747 is much loved for its incredibly smooth landing characteristics and gentle handling and flight, the 787 uses a latest technology known as 'smooth ride' to counteract turbulence in flight. This is the same technology that the 777X will use when it finally debuts in 2027. Although the 747 was known as the Queen of the Skies, the Dreamliner has become the best-selling widebody in history. It has been the flagship product of the legendary plane maker, as its 737 MAX has flailed in the wake of a disastrous debut.

    Recent findings suggest that this is not only a major improvement for the long-haul market, but also for operators that use these aircraft for high-density hub-to-hub transport, and makes a major improvement for the densest routes in the world. A 787 Dreamliner is not only a game-changer for the operators that fly it, but it also marks a paradigm shift in the experience for flyers. While the era of the 747 ushered in a golden age of jet-powered commercial aviation, the 787 and future successors such as the 777X herald the next era in air travel.

    • It has been revealed that fifty years later, Alexander S.C.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sen. Alex Padilla, D-Calif., speaks during a ceremony marking the restoration of Alexander Calder’s Mountains and Clouds sculpture in the Hart Senate Office Building atrium on Wednesday. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call).

    The day after Alexander Calder presented his proposal for a public art display in the Hart Building’s nine-story atrium to the Architect of the Capitol, he died.

    It has been revealed that fifty years later, Alexander S.C. Rower felt a sense of awe as he stared up at his grandfather’s work, finally restored to what he had envisioned.

    “It’s totally phenomenal,” he stated, pointing up at the now-moving clouds as he spoke, spinning his finger around. “It’s not entertainment, but it’s trying to emulate naturalness, trying to emulate what nature would do.”.

    In a recent development, it was a long time coming for Rower, who remembers traveling to the Capitol in his 20s for the original dedication of the Mountains and Clouds sculpture in 1987. The mobile portion stopped rotating as Calder intended in the 1990s, and it was ultimately removed in 2014 after being deemed unsafe by the Architect of the Capitol. Millions of dollars in private philanthropy later, Calder’s clouds are spinning again.

    It has been revealed that rower was back on the Hill on Wednesday for an event celebrating the restoration, joining Architect of the Capitol Thomas Austin, Sens. Alex Padilla, D-Calif., Angus King, I-Maine, and James Lankford, R-Okla., and the project’s donors. As the speakers addressed the crowd, the clouds began to speed up slightly. Onlookers gathered on the balconies overlooking the atrium and peeked through office windows. Attendees left with tote bags emblazoned with images of Calder’s art.

    According to Rower, who leads the Calder Foundation dedicated to preserving and interpreting his grandfather’s art, the mobile is rotating on a 15-hour cycle that is “totally variable.”.

    “It can go a little faster; it can go a little slower,” he mentioned. “I told the team today that during lunchtime, I want it to speed up just a little bit because everyone’s going to lunch. There’ll be … a lot of activity passing through, and then right at 2:30, well, let’s make it go quieter.”.

    It was a labor of love for those involved, and not an inexpensive one. Jon and Kim Shirley funded the $12 million restoration. Because the pieces were so large, they were transported on an extra-wide load truck and driven at a speed of 35 miles per hour from Michigan.

    It has been revealed that “We had to call every senator or governor that we knew on that route, which went through seven states, to get permissions,” he mentioned. “That was a huge thing to overcome, and it all happened over a weekend. So my wife was actually on the phone with a governor’s wife on Saturday evening. The next day, he called up his Department of Transportation and got a permit.”.

    Christian Quilici, who helped manage the project on behalf of the Shirleys and noted he serves as a liaison between the foundation and Congress, said the hardest part of the project was the size of it.

    “We had to tear the wall down on C Street, which nobody really thought of in the beginning,” he mentioned. “Nobody got how big this was until it highlighted up on their doorstep.”.

    Quilici said he spent years educating at least 30 different senators about the quest to reunite the mobile with the stationary mountains left behind. Some of the biggest champions were seated in the front row at Wednesday’s event, including Senate Democratic Whip Richard J. Durbin. Absent was Sen. Christopher S. Murphy, D-Conn., who has been away from the Capitol while recovering from a stroke but has been a supporter of the sculpture’s restoration for years, pressing former acting Architect of the Capitol Joseph DiPietro on it at a 2024 Senate Legislative Branch Appropriations budget hearing.

    “Is there any chance that before I leave the Senate, or at least before I die, we can get the clouds back up there?” Murphy mentioned at the time.

    Padilla read a letter on Wednesday from Murphy, whose state was Calder’s home for much of his life.

    Recent findings suggest that “This statue is actually a statement on our democracy, that we have big pieces of monumental art right in the middle of our most key and most iconic government buildings. To get this piece of art restored to how it was designed by the artist, well, that’s good for Connecticut. But I also like to think … it’s good for democracy too,” Murphy’s statement said.

    The restoration was funded entirely by donations from the Shirleys, who are prominent Calder collectors, according to Rower.

    “It’s very emotional to see the work completed after 10 years of us working so hard with the Architect of the Capitol and Calder Foundation. It’s a very overpowering, overwhelming emotion,” said Kim Shirley.

    It has been revealed that in addition to helping fund the project, she’s a former Senate staffer who worked in Hart before Calder’s work was installed. Years after her time in the Senate was over, her husband Jon wanted to show her the sculpture, now filling the space she used to walk through every day.

    According to recent reports, but when the two arrived, the clouds weren’t hanging from the ceiling like they were supposed to be. He called up Rower, who was a friend of his, and said he wanted to get them back to how Calder intended. On Wednesday, the three of them stood together in Hart, looking up.

    Technological and engineering advancements allowed for newer, lighter clouds to be built and be safe to hang from the ceiling.

    “Before it was like a bulb, it looked like a hoagie sandwich, and now it looks just really sharp, like a razor cutting through space, which was Calder’s intention,” Rower remarked.

    In a recent development, according to Rower, it involved laser-measuring the original model of Mountains and Clouds sitting in a glass case nearby in the Hart atrium. The newly introduced clouds, he said, are made of carbon fiber.

    “These are giant things up in the air, and they’re just so gentle and subtle,” he said.

    Younger Hill staffers don’t know a time with clouds. But for those who have spent decades in the building, it was a special moment to see them spin, as Lankford told the crowd.

    “I can’t tell you how many tour groups that I’ve walked through this building and I pointed to this, and I remarked it’s only half there, and would take them over to the little model that’s right over here, and say this is what it’s supposed to look like,” said the senator, a former Hill staffer himself.

    Standing under his grandfather’s sculpture, Rower found himself quoting the man responsible for it all.

    “I find that everything I do, if it is made for a particular spot, is more successful,” he noted, gazing up at it.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Emirates is known for being a world-class airline, though at this point, the carrier’s ground experience at Dubai International Airport (DXB) leaves a lot to be desired, especially for premium passengers.

    Recent findings suggest that while I don’t want to suggest that the carrier’s first class lounges and business class lounges are terrible, they’re far from cutting edge, and the design definitely feels extremely outdated. Earlier this year, I wrote a post asking if Emirates was going to revamp its lounges at the airport, or just wait until the theoretical move to Dubai World Central (DWC) around 2032.

    Well, it seems that my concerns have now been addressed, as Emirates has confirmed intends to completely transform its lounge experience in Dubai. Over the summer we saw the airline start to roll out a newly introduced global lounge concept for outstation lounges, and that idea is now coming to Dubai as well.

    It has been revealed that as is the case for any airline, rolling out a new lounge concept at a hub airport isn’t easy, given that it requires spaces to be closed. So that’s why it’s worth noting that Emirates is taking an innovative approach to refreshing its lounges in Dubai:.

    Sources indicate that emirates is investing a total of 400 million AED ($109 million) in these lounge spaces. Interestingly, Emirates claims that “all flagship lounges” will be getting a redesign, though there’s zero mention of the lounges in Concourse A, which are the biggest lounges in the world (they span the entire concourse), and offer direct boarding to planes. So it’s not clear when those lounges will undergo updates.

    Here’s how Emirates President Tim Clark describes this development:.

    Recent findings suggest that “Our customers expect the very best from Emirates, whether while flying or spending time with us on the ground. We believe the airport experience should be every bit as exceptional as the journey itself, and that’s why we are transforming our lounges globally. This new First Class Lounge in Dubai is the first taste of what’s to come. And if these are the lengths we will go to for a temporary lounge… just imagine what you can expect from new Emirates Lounges going forward. Over the next two years, we’ll be unveiling a completely different lounge experience, with new concepts in dining, wellness, entertainment and personalised hospitality. We’re going well beyond a traditional refurbishment and creating extraordinary spaces.”.

    We’ve already seen how Emirates is overhauling its global lounge network, and I’d say the changes are pretty awesome. So what can we expect in Dubai? As you can see, Clark references how the temporary new first class lounge is just a small glimpse into what we can expect in the future. Below is a video showing the new concept, and I must say, it looks impressive!

    Here’s how Emirates describes the lounge concept, broadly:.

    Featuring immersive culinary experiences to dedicated wellness facilities and innovative entertainment concepts, Emirates is redefining what customers can expect from their time at the airport. Building on Emirates’ renowned hospitality, customers can expect distinct spaces for dining, relaxation, work and socialising – complemented by intuitive technology, refined interiors and elevated personal service. Each lounge will bear the hallmarks of the iconic Emirates brand, with the interiors conveying luxury, comfort, exceptional hospitality and global appeal.

    When it comes to the temporary new first class lounge, here are the details:.

    As much as people like to suggest that Gulf carriers just throw money down the drain when it comes to passenger experience, Emirates is actually a pretty disciplined and cost focused business, which is also clear based on the fact that the airline still has angled business class seats with seven seats per row. 😉.

    But when the airline does invest and upgrade its products, it has a pretty good sense of what customers like. Barista coffee, Dom Perignon, and a gym? Count me in (though maybe the amenities shouldn’t be enjoyed in that order). 😉 It does sound like there still won’t be dedicated bedrooms, which would be disappointing, but also wouldn’t surprise me, given the volume of rooms they’d need to serve guests.

    Two things stand out to me here:.

    It has been revealed that emirates is hugely investing in its lounge network in Dubai, something that’s long overdue, if you ask me. Over the next two years, at least four lounges will be getting a full makeover, to match the carrier’s new lounge aesthetic.

    We’ve just seen the opening of a new temporarily first class lounge in Concourse B, which is described as an example of what’s to come. Next year that lounge is expected to become a business class lounge, as a new flagship first class lounge opens, along with additional first and business class lounges.

    Industry observers note that the upcoming design aesthetic looks great, and it sounds like some thought is being put into amenities as well. I look forward to seeing this transformation, though I can’t help but wonder if this reflects a delay with Emirates moving to its new hub airport.

    Tech Report: Citi Shop offers an easier way to save when shopping online

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • According to recent reports, citi Shop takes some of the work out of saving money online.
    • It has broad reach, too, with more than 5,000 participating online merchants.
    • Its ease of use makes it a great resource, but other portals or special discounts may save you more.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, citi Shop takes some of the work out of saving money online. Once you've installed its browser extension, it acts as a shopping portal and coupon hunter all-in-one, rewarding you with statement credits.

    It has broad reach, too, with more than 5,000 participating online merchants. That's easier than a traditional online shopping portal, which requires you to remember to start at the portal and click through before filling your cart.

    Its ease of use makes it a great resource, but other portals or special discounts may save you more.

    Here's how Citi Shop works and what to consider to determine if it's the best savings path for you.

    Citi Shop is a free browser extension for primary cardholders with an eligible Citi credit card, including ThankYou points cards and cobranded cards. Citi retail and commercial cards are usually ineligible.

    Offers come as either a percentage back or a fixed amount back, and your earnings are applied as a statement credit on the Citi card you selected during enrollment.

    Citi Shop is separate from Citi Merchant Offers, which requires you to enroll in targeted offers with a specific Citi card and then use that card for the qualifying purchase.

    Both Citi Shop and traditional portals give you an extra reward for making purchases they track.

    But Citi Shop brings potential rebates to you, rather than requiring you to initiate your savings search. The extension automatically displays a pop-up with an available offer when you visit a participating website. You'll have the option to activate the offer before checkout.

    All of Citi Shop's rebates are provided as statement credits, unlike the potential airline miles, hotel points or credit card rewards of traditional portals.

    Sources indicate that what I like about Citi Shop is that it also acts like a shopping assistant. Instead of opening six coupon sites only to discover that every code expired last Tuesday, it handles the scavenger hunt for you and tests available promo codes on your behalf.

    In a recent development, like Capital One Shopping, Citi Shop uses a browser extension. However, Capital One Shopping doesn't require a Capital One card to enroll and its rewards can be redeemed for eligible gift cards instead of a statement credit.

    Generally speaking, Citi Shop clashes with other shopping portals. Both work by referring and tracking your purchase, so they can be mutually exclusive. You'll need to make your purchase through whichever offer is better.

    Related: Chase shopping portal guide: How to earn bonus Ultimate Rewards points.

    Industry observers note that unless Citi Shop finds a promo code, it won't lower your total at checkout. Its returns arrive later as statement credits and may require patiently waiting two to six months, sometimes longer.

    In a recent development, even though you need an eligible Citi card to enroll, you don’t have to pay with it. Citi allows any payment method accepted by the merchant.

    I really appreciate the flexibility to choose the best card for each purchase. For electronics, I might pick a card with an extended warranty while I might stick to a travel rewards credit card for hotel bookings. You can even pay with a gift card if you wish.

    Regardless of how you pay, the statement credit will post to the Citi card you enrolled.

    If you have an eligible Citi card but rarely remember to click through a shopping portal, Citi Shop is an easy win. Install it, activate offers when the pop-up appears and let the credits come to you. That convenience can also be a big benefit if you have partners or other family members who aren't as motivated to strategize on rewards as you are.

    But with a little extra effort, you might be able to earn even more. When the Citi Shop pop-up appears with an offer, take a minute to compare before you click Activate.

    Checking a shopping portal aggregator such as Cashback Monitor highlights payouts from multiple cash-back, airline and credit card portals, making it easier to compare a Citi Shop statement credit with points or miles elsewhere.

    Suppose a $200 jacket is marked down to $160. Citi Shop finds a $10 coupon, bringing the checkout price to $150, and offers 8% back. Assuming the full amount qualifies, you'd receive a $12 Citi Shop credit. If you pay with a card that earns 2% back and has an activated merchant offer for $5 off a $100 purchase, you'd collect another $8. After all the credits and rewards post, your net cost would be $130.

    It has been revealed that read the terms before getting too excited. Some brands, products, gift cards or coupon codes may be excluded and you might not be able to stack every layer every time. Still, you can often use multiple discounts simultaneously for a better deal.

    Sources indicate that citi Shop is not a program for instant gratification. Citi states statement credits post 61 to 180 days after a completed purchase, though some can take longer.

    In many cases, offers may show as pending long before they officially pay out, to account for potential returns. Hotel rewards may remain pending until after the stay. Eventually, you'll see it on your statement as "CITI SHOP STATEMENT CREDIT.".

    If a credit hasn't posted after the expected window, contact Citi using the number on the back of your enrolled card. You may want to keep good records along the way, like a screenshot of the offer and an e-receipt from the purchase.

    Citi Shop's biggest advantage is convenience. It does the heavy lifting by reminding you to activate offers so you don't miss out on earnings from your online orders, while testing coupon codes along the way. The offers themselves may or may not be the highest available, but they are certainly the easiest.

    In a recent development, to truly optimize your returns, you'll want to compare Citi Shop earnings with those from other shopping portals — and stack other forms of saving along the way. But when that sounds like too much, the ease of this extension can still be a great way to tack on some extra returns.
